title: Find the Sequence of Strings Appeared on the Screen
statement:
A screen starts out empty, and the keyboard has only two keys:

- key 1 adds the letter `'a'` to the end of the text on the screen;
- key 2 replaces the last letter of the text with the following letter of the alphabet (`'z'` turns into `'a'`).

On an empty screen only key 1 does anything useful. The string `target` is typed using the fewest key presses possible. Return the texts shown on the screen right after each of those key presses, in the order they appear (the last one is `target` itself).
constraints: target contains only lowercase English letters
Local cases keep the answer within the app's 256 KiB output limit (for example, at most 138 letters when every letter is z)
notes:
## Intuition

Neither key can delete anything, and key 2 only touches the last letter. So letters are settled from left to right: once key 1 appends the next `'a'`, the letter before it can never change again. Each letter of `target` therefore costs one key-1 press, which shows an `'a'`, followed by key-2 presses that walk that last letter forward until it matches. Walking from `'a'` up to the letter takes `letter - 'a'` presses, and going around past `'z'` would only add 26 more, so the fewest-presses typing never wraps and is unique. The answer is just the screen after every press.

## Approach

1. `screens` collects the answer; `typed` is the finished part of `target`.
2. For each `letter` of `target`, press key 1: `last` becomes `'a'`, and `typed + last` is recorded.
3. While `last` is not `letter`, press key 2: move `last` one letter on and record `typed + last`.
4. Add `letter` to `typed` and continue. Return `screens`.

## Example 1, step by step

`target = "abc"`. For `a`, key 1 shows `"a"`, which already matches. For `b`, key 1 shows `"aa"` and one key 2 shows `"ab"`. For `c`, key 1 shows `"aba"`, then key 2 twice shows `"abb"` and `"abc"`. So `screens = ["a", "aa", "ab", "aba", "abb", "abc"]`.

## Complexity

- Time: O(26 · n²) for `n = target.length`: up to 26 screens per letter, each a new string of up to `n` characters. The answer itself has that size, so no method can do better.
- Space: the same for the answer; only O(n) beyond it.

## Pitfalls

- Record the screen after every press, including the key-1 press that shows `'a'` even when `'a'` is the wanted letter.
- Finish each letter before pressing key 1 again; after that it is frozen.
- Never wrap around: counting forward from `'a'` is always shortest.
- In languages with mutable character buffers, store a fresh copy for each screen, not the same buffer again and again.

## Variables

| Name | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `screens` | the texts shown so far, in order |
| `typed` | the finished part of `target` |
| `letter` | the letter of `target` being typed |
| `last` | the current last letter on the screen |

narration.2: Every text shown on the screen is collected here, in order.
narration.3: The part of target that is already finished on the screen.
narration.4: Type target one letter at a time, from left to right.
narration.6: Record the screen right after that key 1 press.
narration.7: Press key 2 until the last letter is right; starting from a, no wrap past z is ever needed.
narration.8: Key 2 moves the last letter one step along the alphabet.
narration.9: Record the screen after this key 2 press.
narration.11: This letter is final: the next key 1 press freezes it.
narration.13: Return the screens in the order they appeared.
